summary:
Ex0thermic is an interactive, SI-powered dashboard designed to uncover critical fire-safety insights from decades of NASA microgravity experiments.

Using real NASA PSI datasets (Saffire-II, BASS-II, FLEX-035, and SAME-R), our platform enables engineers and mission planners to rapidly search, rank, and visualize flame spread rates, PMMA thermal limits, cool-flame droplet burning, and smoke particle aging. Unlike conventional generative AI that risks fabricating engineering numbers, Aerofox integrates an open-weight language model with deterministic physics engines and a robust rule-based fallback mode, ensuring every chart, unit conversion, and NASA-STD-6001B compliance check is 100% reproducible and traceable to SHA-256 verified source files. We built an end-to-end workflow: auditing raw PSI workbooks, resolving published airflow discrepancies, evaluating EVA suit and lunar rover risks, and simulating multi-zone smoke propagation across habitat ventilation layouts.

This matters because a single fire in deep space can be catastrophic. By bridging archived combustion data and deterministic modeling, Aerofox reduces design uncertainty and protects astronaut lives on the Moon and Mars.
details:
What Ex0therm does

Ex0therm is an evidence-grounded assistant designed to help engineers and researchers explore, audit and interpret microgravity combustion data for spacecraft fire safety. The application allows users to ask questions about NASA’s reduced-gravity fire experiments, compare experiments runs, evaluate whether a given atmosphere is represented in the data, create figures and charts and identify what additional measurements and validation tests would be needed before a spacecraft design decision could be justified. Rather than acting as a general-purpose chatbot, Ex0therm strictly separates three types of output: (a) reported observations and reprocessed data, (b) deterministic calculations based on declared physical assumptions, and (c) qualitative engineering synthesis from na LLM or a rule-based fallback.

How does it work

Ex0therm combines a locally running Large Language Model (LLM) with a curated NASA scientific database and deterministic Python-based analysis tools.

  • Data inventory: The primary archive is NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI), investigation discovery used the PSI search API for the combustion-science research area, study metadata, experiment tables and file catalogs were retrieved separately; NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) supplied contextual publications and reported results not present in the small tables. The acquisition code builds a local inventory manifest containing canonical URLs, file sizes, content types, retrieval timestamps, and SHA-256 checksums. The published code distinguishes acquisition from analysis, and the notebook consumes the processed snapshot and regenerates the figures and findings, which isn’t the same thing as the original PSI payload.
  • Data quality: The system ingests raw experiment tables and processes them into analysis-ready formats, enforcing standard scientific units (converting pressures to kPa and oxygen to mole fractions (0-1) and flags anomalous or missing cells instead of silently replacing them with zeros.

Critical data layout issues are resolved programmatically (such as reconciling an official numbering mismatch affecting 119 of 274 FLEX experiment table rows using cross-references Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) identifiers to align droplet records with their correct test runs, drastically improving analytical reliability.

  • Retrieval and conversation state management: User sessions maintain validated project attributes (vehicle type, pressure, oxygen fraction, gravity, and materials), recent conversation context, artifact registry and lock. Queries are matched against a local SQLite FTS5 evidence store (containing 90 curated entries and 38 processed tables) using BM25 ranking, Unicode/Porter tokenization, and bilingual (English-Portuguese) synonym expansion.
  • Local Open-Model and Tool Orchestration: To support real-world demonstrations, AeroFox v1.1.2 introduces asynchronous request processing with live progress updates, a visible queue for up to six waiting requests, persistent SQLite sessions, and a process supervisor that monitors and restarts failed services. A stable HTTPS address is provided through Tailscale Funnel, allowing external users to access the locally hosted assistant while the host computer remains online.
  • Deterministic Calculation and Synthesis: All numerical fits, unit conversions, atmosphere comparisons, and multizone passive-tracer transport equations (solved via Backward Euler and RK4 with the network residual report below 10⁻⁹ under the test definition) are executed exclusively by verified Python functions. The model then synthesizes a concise, source-cited explanation accompanied by Plotly graphs, qualitative matrices, Mermaid verification flowcharts, and CSV exports. If inference fails or times out, a deterministic fallback ensures the calculated charts and evidence cards are still delivered

What benefits does it have

Ex0therm offers several key benefits driven by its neurosymbolic design and rigorous data auditing. First, it reduces the risk of numerical hallucinations by separating language generation from validated scientific calculations because the orchestrator checks language and intent before deciding between model-backed generation and a deterministic path, utilizing tools with argument validations, time limits, and fixed output types where models cite retrieved source identifiers to reduce fabrication. Second, the system enables the correction of hidden archival errors by uncovering and resolving critical flaws in raw NASA archives, such as fixing FLEX table row misalignments which improved the burning-rate correlation with tabular constants from r = 0.729 to r = 0.987 —and identifying that Saffire-II sample 2-6 experienced an actual telemetry-measured airflow of ~25 cm/s despite being listed as 20 cm/s in the nominal table. Third, it provides nuanced microgravity insights that allow users to instantly explore complex physical phenomena, such as continued heptane droplet regression after visible hot-flame extinction in FLEX-035 or smoke particle size distributions across materials like Kapton, Teflon, and Silicone in SAME-R. Finally, it improves operational resilience and keeps model inference and the scientific data snapshot under the team's local control because both the local data snapshot and the quantized Qwen weights execute entirely on the user's machine, requiring no live external API keys or continuous connection to NASA servers while enabling browser-based public demonstrations through a stable Tailscale Funnel HTTPS address, supported by automatic process recovery and asynchronous request handling.

Tools, coding languages, hardware, or software used to develop the project?

  • Programming Languages: Python (3.11 / 3.12), SQL (SQLite FTS5), and Windows Batch scripting (START_AEROFOX.bat).
  • AI Models & Inference Engine: llama.cpp running open-weight quantized GGUF models: Qwen3-4B (Q4_K_M, ~2.50 GB) and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (Q4_K_M, ~1.12 GB).
  • Data Sources & Standards: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) search API and datasets) NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS).
  • Hardware & Deployment: Windows laptop equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 3050 GPU (6 GB VRAM); Python/FastAPI backend; SQLite for evidence retrieval and session persistence; Plotly for interactive scientific visualizations; llama.cpp for local inference; a Python process supervisor for automatic recovery; and Tailscale Funnel for HTTPS public access.
  • Verification: 74 automated Python tests and 25 browser checks passed in the reported development environment. On the Windows demonstration host, three concurrent user requests were successfully completed using the local Qwen model, and application/model recovery was tested through controlled process failures.

How is yours project creative

Ex0therm introduces a distinctive approach to scientific AI for spacecraft fire safety by combining independent language-model inference, reproducible numerical analysis, and critical auditing of original NASA experimental data. Instead of using AI in a conventional, passive way, the project creates an original solution that bridges complex raw data with uncompromising scientific rigor. Its creativity is anchored in four fundamental pillars. First, it implements a hybrid neuro-symbolic architecture (the "dual brain"): while typical generative AI models attempt to guess answers through free text, which is dangerous in fire safety, Ex0therm rigidly separates functions, delegating all mathematical calculations, droplet burning-rate equations (D2), and standard verifications to a deterministic Python physics engine, while the language model acts solely as an intent translator and tool planner to reduce unsupported numerical claims and keep structured calculations traceable to their inputs and scientific sources.

Second, the project demonstrates technical creativity through active auditing and data correction: rather than blindly downloading NASA PSI files, the team audited and corrected hidden historical inconsistencies in official archives..

Third, Ex0therm introduces radical transparency and evidence-gap management: creating an assistant that knows how to say what it doesn't know is a profound software innovation. The system enforces strict evidence labels (Measured, Derived, Synthetic, Published Interpretation) and, if an exploration atmosphere (like lunar or Martian targets) lacks direct solid-material test data, it refuses to fabricate numeric risk scores, instead clearly presenting the evidence gap alongside a structured verification plan.

What factors did your team consider?

To ensure scientific rigor and engineering reliability, our team structured observational units carefully—distinguishing between file entries, experiment table rows, FLEX droplet runs, Saffire samples, and SAME-R smoke tests without pooling them as independent replicates. Using ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions and 2,000-resample bootstrap intervals, the system models burning-rate constants (K) against oxygen fractions, pressures, and diluents while accounting for non-factorial design confounding. Rather than relying solely on surface-level metadata, AeroFox incorporates deep investigations of historical anomalies, including FLEX-035 (exposing continued droplet regression for roughly 25 seconds after visible hot-flame extinction), Saffire-II (reconciling nominal table data with actual 1 Hz telemetry airflow), BASS-II (examining 129 tabular test-point records while distinguishing them from the 126 conducted tests reported in NASA's summary), and SAME-R (summarizing particle size distributions across materials like Kapton and Teflon while noting detector saturation limits).

Supporting the transition from Earth-orbiting standards (101.3 kPa, 21% O2) to reduced-pressure exploration atmospheres (such as 56.5 kPa / 34% O2 for Artemis) required mapping archived PSI experiments against exploration targets. Using strict proximity windows (+/- 10kPa and +/- 0.03 O2 mole fraction), AeroFox explicitly identifies where direct solid-material test data is missing, preventing engineers from misapplying liquid-droplet or nominal-flow data to solid habitats. Furthermore, because gravity, total pressure, oxygen partial pressure (pO2), fuel geometry, and forced convection interact non-linearly, we designed the system to evaluate physical applicability strictly per subsystem—such as separating an EVA suit's breathing volume from its internal oxygen circuit and electrical compartments.

Finally, we prioritized data provenance, operational reliability, and transparent boundaries. Every ingested file is tracked via canonical URLs, fetch timestamps, and SHA-256 hashes, with license terms (such as CC0-1.0 versus unlabelled records like PSI-10) documented and non-redistributable telemetry workbooks represented via traceable derived data windows. To guarantee smooth execution on standard hardware, we implemented automatic GPU/CPU profile switching, deterministic fallback modes, per-session state locks, strict input validation, CSV formula-injection hardening, and a strict browser Content Security Policy. Crucially, our team bounded all project claims—explicitly defining AeroFox as an exploratory research and preliminary design-review aid rather than a CFD flame-spread solver, a certified material qualification database, or an autonomous spacecraft fire-control computer.

What is the intended impact of the project?

AeroFox bridges the critical gap between raw archival microgravity research and early-stage spacecraft safety engineering. Through its exploratory analysis of combustion data, the system structures observational units without improper pooling and models burning-rate constants (K) against oxygen fractions, pressures, and diluents using ordinary least squares regressions and bootstrap intervals. This ensures that engineers do not rely on surface-level metadata or make false equivalencies between disparate experimental designs.

Furthermore, by integrating reproducible scientific case studies—such as uncovering continued droplet regression after visible hot-flame extinction in FLEX-035, reconciling nominal versus telemetry-measured airflow in Saffire-II, and summarizing smoke particle size distributions in SAME-R—the project provides deep empirical grounding for complex microgravity phenomena.

As human spaceflight transitions from Earth-orbiting platforms (101.3 kPa, 21% O2) toward reduced-pressure, oxygen-enriched exploration habitats (such as 56.5 kPa / 34% O2 for Artemis and Mars missions), AeroFox maps archived NASA experiments against these exploration targets. Using strict proximity windows, the project explicitly identifies where direct solid-material test data is missing, preventing engineers from misapplying liquid-droplet or nominal-flow data to solid habitats. Ultimately, its intended impact is to accelerate preliminary design reviews, eliminate blind data extrapolation, and generate structured verification workflows that identify exactly what empirical evidence must be gathered before justifying a spacecraft safety decision.

AI-assisted development tools, including Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, were used to support data-analysis workflows, software implementation, testing, interface refinement, and deployment configuration. The scientific calculations are performed by the project's Python tools, while the deployed conversational assistant uses independently hosted open-weight models.
